answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1858–1947 · German theoretical physicist, founder of quantum theory
answer.sourceLine: Planck wrote it in German in his 1946 memoir essay “Persönliche Erinnerungen aus alten Zeiten” and reused it in his Wissenschaftliche Selbstbiographie (1948). This exact English is Frank Gaynor’s translation in Scientific Autobiography and Other Papers (1949), pp. 33–34, as Quote Investigator confirms ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Frank Gaynor, 1949 (Philosophical Library, New York), pp. 33–34
“Persönliche Erinnerungen aus alten Zeiten,” Die Naturwissenschaften 33, no. 8 (30 Oct. 1946), p. 235

source.excerpt: A new scientific truth does not triumph by convincing its opponents and making them see the light, but rather because its opponents eventually die, and a new generation grows up that is familiar with it.
trail: 1946 — Planck publishes the German sentence in “Persönliche Erinnerungen aus alten Zeiten,” Die Naturwissenschaften, 30 October 1946 (Quote Investigator ↗).
1948 — The passage appears in his Wissenschaftliche Selbstbiographie (Barth, Leipzig), p. 22 (Wikiquote ↗).

1949 — Frank Gaynor’s English translation, Scientific Autobiography and Other Papers, is published by Philosophical Library in New York (Internet Archive record ↗). It contains the popular wording on pp. 33–34.

1962 onward — Thomas S. Kuhn quotes the Gaynor sentence in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions. In 1975 Paul Samuelson boils it down to “science makes progress funeral by funeral” (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: Planck’s German, as Wikiquote gives it ↗: “Eine neue wissenschaftliche Wahrheit pflegt sich nicht in der Weise durchzusetzen, daß ihre Gegner überzeugt werden und sich als belehrt erklären, sondern vielmehr dadurch, daß ihre Gegner allmählich aussterben und daß die heranwachsende Generation von vornherein mit der Wahrheit vertraut gemacht ist.” Wikiquote also prints a different English rendering, “revised by Eric Weinberger.” So the popular wording is one translation, not the only one.

author.name: Max Planck
author.heading: About Max Planck
author.bio: Max Planck was the German physicist whose work on black-body radiation founded quantum theory, and he won the Nobel Prize in Physics. Late in life he wrote short memoirs about his career. In them he looked back on how slowly his early ideas on thermodynamics were accepted, and that is where this remark about how new ideas win comes from.

misattribution.heading: The quote is real, but its short forms are not Planck’s
misattribution.intro: Planck really wrote this long sentence. It is the shortened, punchier versions credited to him that he never wrote.

items.who: “Science advances one funeral at a time”
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ lists this under “Paraphrased variants” beneath Planck’s passage. It is not in his text.

items.who: “Science makes progress funeral by funeral” (Paul A. Samuelson)
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the compact “funeral by funeral” form in the economist Paul Samuelson’s writing, starting in Newsweek on 16 June 1975. Samuelson credited the idea to Planck, but the phrasing is Samuelson’s.

items.who: “Truth never triumphs — its opponents just die out”
items.why: Wikiquote also lists this line, and its German form “Die Wahrheit triumphiert nie, ihre Gegner sterben nur aus,” as paraphrased variants (Wikiquote ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The full sentence is Planck’s own, in Frank Gaynor’s 1949 translation of his Scientific Autobiography, pp. 33–34 (Quote Investigator ↗). The short “funeral” versions came later.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Planck was writing about his own career, and about how slowly his early ideas won acceptance. The sentence then took on a life of its own. Thomas S. Kuhn cited it in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), and it came to be called “Planck’s principle”: the idea that scientific change follows generational turnover rather than persuasion alone (Wikipedia ↗).

Economists later tested it. Pierre Azoulay, Christian Fons-Rosen and Joshua Graff Zivin’s paper “Does Science Advance One Funeral at a Time?” (American Economic Review, August 2019) found that after star scientists died, their collaborators published less in the field, while newcomers’ activity rose (Wikipedia summary ↗).
context.pull: Its opponents eventually die, and a new generation grows up that is familiar with it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Exact English wording is in Gaynor's translation of Planck's Scientific Autobiography, pp. 33-34; German original in Die Naturwissenschaften 33(8), 30 Oct 1946, p. 235; Kuhn cited it in 1962; Samuelson's 'funeral by funeral' from Newsweek 16 June 1975

German passage cited to Wissenschaftliche Selbstbiographie (Barth, Leipzig 1948) p. 22 and Gaynor 1949 pp. 33-34; alternative translation revised by Eric Weinberger; 'Science advances one funeral at a time' and 'Truth never triumphs...' listed as paraphrased variants
Scientific autobiography and other papers, Planck (1858-1947), Philosophical Library, New York, 1949, with Gaynor as an associated name

The passage is the basis of 'Planck's principle', cited by Kuhn; Azoulay, Fons-Rosen and Graff Zivin, 'Does Science Advance One Funeral at a Time?', AER Aug 2019, found collaborators' output fell and non-collaborators' activity rose after star scientists died
